Let Them Cook
LET THEM KOOK
phrase (Gen Alpha slang)
From cook in the slang sense "to perform brilliantly" (sports and hip-hop: "he’s cooking"), the phrase "let him cook" — let him keep going, he’s onto something — spread through sports commentary, streams, and TikTok around 2022–23, often for someone doing something strange that might turn out brilliant. Gen Alpha says "let him cook" or "let them cook" to defend a friend’s unusual plan; its opposite is cooked (done for, ruined).

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

"Let him cook!" means "Give him a chance — he’s doing something, and it might be great." Gen Alpha kids say it when a friend has a strange plan or starts something surprising. The Christian observation: the phrase carries a small virtue worth keeping — patience with someone’s work before you judge it. Scripture says love "suffereth long, and is kind" (1Co 13:4), and warns against judging too fast: "He that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame unto him" (Pro 18:13). Letting someone finish is a kind of love. And the phrase has a beautiful theological echo. God is the One who "cooks" in our lives, doing slow work we cannot see yet: "he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ" (Php 1:6); "we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works" (Eph 2:10). When a child is still learning and growing, a wise father says, "Let him cook — God is not finished with him." And Scripture even has a kitchen story about it: Martha, busy cooking, was reminded that Mary had "chosen that good part" by sitting at Jesus’s feet (Luk 10:42). A father can tell a five-year-old: "Let’s let your sister finish her drawing before we say anything — let her cook! God is patient with us while we learn, too."

Webster 1828 Definition

Slang (c. 2022–23) from cook = perform brilliantly: give someone room to finish — a small virtue of patience, and an echo of the God who finishes the good work He begins.

expand to see more

LET THEM COOK, phr. (sports and internet slang, c. 2022–present; Gen Alpha) Let them continue; they might be onto something. Also let him cook, let her cook. "He’s building a ramp out of couch cushions — let him cook."

Related: cooking (performing well), cooked (done for).

Decode for parents: harmless, and often kind.

Webster 1828, the root — COOK, v.t. To prepare, as victuals for the table, by boiling, roasting, baking, broiling, etc.

Key Scripture

1Co 13:4 — "Charity suffereth long, and is kind; charity envieth not; charity vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up,"

Pro 18:13 — "He that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame unto him."

Php 1:6 — "Being confident of this very thing, that he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ:"

Eph 2:10 — "For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them."

Luk 10:42 — "But one thing is needful: and Mary hath chosen that good part, which shall not be taken away from her."

Modern Corruption

"Let them cook" is a mostly kind phrase of patience with another’s work; its only caution is excusing a plan that is plainly foolish because it looks bold.

expand to see more

There is little to correct. Occasionally the phrase defends something that should be stopped — a dangerous stunt, a cruel prank — under the banner of creativity. Not everything bold is good, and wisdom sometimes says "do not let him cook."

Mostly, keep it. Teach children to hear before judging and to give each other room to try. Then teach the theology: God’s patient workmanship in us is the real "let him cook." A family that is slow to criticize and quick to encourage is practicing 1 Corinthians 13 at the kitchen table.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin coquere (to cook) → English cook → slang cooking (performing brilliantly) → "let him cook" (c. 2022–23).

"Charity suffereth long — let her finish (1Co 13:4)."
